## 1 Introduction and Related Works

Data denoising is a fundamental problem arising in many areas of data science, signal processing, control theory, and machine learning. Denoisers have been successfully applied to signal processing (Kailath et al., 2000), image processing (Hirakawa and Parks, 2006; Zhang et al., 2017; Zamir et al., 2022) and generative AI (Song et al., ; Song and Ermon, 2019) .

Arguably the most widely known denoiser, the Wiener Filter (Wiener, 1964; Kolmogorov, 1941), dates back to the 1940s. However, constructing such filter in practice requires precise knowledge of the covariance of the data $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Noting that reliable estimation of the second-order statistics requires access to plethora of samples, other works, such as Hirakawa and Parks (2006), attempt to circumvent such need by learning denoisers directly from data.

To provide a pertinent and opportune motivation, denoisers are used as central building blocks in modern diffusion models (Song et al., ; Song and Ermon, 2019). In the context of diffusion, the denoiser $D_{\bm{\theta}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is a neural network parametrized by its weights $\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ , such as UNet (Ho et al., 2020) or Diffusion Transformer (DiT) (Peebles and Xie, 2023). Simplifying and omitting certain technical details for ease of explanation, one can illustrate the core idea of denoising diffusion models as follows. Suppose we trained the denoiser $D_{\bm{\theta}}$ to learn a “good quality” approximation $D_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}+\mathbf{z}_{i})\approx\mathbf{x}_{i}$ where $\mathbf{z}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d})$ is artificially injected noise such that the signal to noise ratio (SNR) is very low, i.e.

$$ \displaystyle d\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{2}\approx\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|^{2}\gg\|\mathbf{x}_{i}\|_{2}^{2} $$

Then, under (1), it would be reasonable to attempt generating new samples by dropping dependence of the denoiser on $\mathbf{x}$ as $\mathbf{x}\sim D_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{z})\text{ where }\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d})$ .

Motivated by classical works on learning denoisers as well as more recent works on diffusion, we would like to initiate a systematic study of the performances of denoisers. As a starting point, we propose to study linear denoisers trained via the least squares objective. If the number of samples $n$ and the dimensionality of data $d$ satisfy $n\gg d$ , it is known that the least squares solution will converge to the Wiener Filter, whose performance has been studied extensively in the literature. As such, to make the problem interesting, we assume that $n$ is proportional to $d$ .

In the proportional regime $n$ , the number of samples, and $d$ , the number of features, grow together such that $\frac{n}{d}\rightarrow\kappa$ . This is different from classical works in statistics and control theory, where, usually, $d$ is fixed and $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Arguably, the main technical difference between the two is that one can reliably estimate the covariance of the data reliably when $n\gg d^{2}$ , but, generally speaking, cannot do so if $n=\theta(d)$ . The latter in particular means that the Wiener Filter cannot be recovered precisely in the proportional regime, as it is defined based on the covariance of the data.

Understanding the precise asymptotics of various statistical inference problems in the proportional regime has been the subject of study of many works in the past decade (Thrampoulidis et al., 2018; Mallory et al., 2025; Hastie et al., 2022; Li, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Huang, 2025; Loureiro et al., 2021; Deng et al., 2022; Akhtiamov et al., 2024; Ghane et al., 2025; Akhtiamov et al., 2025b; Ghane et al., 2024). Analyzing the performances of learning algorithms in the proportional regime requires a different toolbox from classical statistical work, the main two of which have proven to be the Approximate Message Passing (AMP) (Donoho et al., 2009) and the Convex Gaussian Min-Max (CGMT) (Thrampoulidis et al., 2014) frameworks. For the purposes of the present work, we employ the latter (CGMT) approach.

## 2 Problem Setting and Preliminaries

We use bold font for vectors and matrices and normal font for scalars in this exposition. Consider the following data denoising problem:

Given $n$ i.i.d data points sampled from the normal distribution $\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\bm{\Sigma})$ with an unknown covariance $\bm{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and a noise distribution $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}})$ with a known covariance $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ , design a linear denoiser $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ , that takes noisy data of the form $\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{z}$ as input and “suppresses the noise” and outputs $\mathbf{W}\hat{\mathbf{x}}\approx\mathbf{x}$ as accurately as possible. More formally, $\mathbf{W}$ should minimize the following generalization error objective: $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}})}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\bm{\Sigma})}\|\mathbf{W}^{T}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{z})-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}$ (2)

Note that (2) can be simplified as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\|(\mathbf{W}^{T}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}=\text{Tr}\left((\mathbf{W}^{T}-\mathbf{I})\bm{\Sigma}(\mathbf{W}^{T}-\mathbf{I})^{T}\right)+\text{Tr}\left(\mathbf{W}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{W}\right) $$

Minimizing (3) over $\mathbf{W}$ directly leads to

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{W}=\left(\bm{\Sigma}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\right)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma} $$

The denoiser (4) is known as the Wiener Filter in the literature. By construction, (4) achieves the optimal generalization error among all linear denoisers. However, finding (4) requires precise knowledge of $\bm{\Sigma}$ . Recovering $\bm{\Sigma}$ from data with good accuracy might not be feasible when $n$ and $d$ are proportional to each other, unlike the classical case $n\gg d$ . As such, one natural approach to the denoising problem would be to take the empirical Wiener Filter

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{W}=\left(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\right)^{-1}\hat{\bm{\Sigma}} $$

Where the empirical covariance $\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}$ is defined as follows via the sample data matrix $\mathbf{X}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{X}^{1}&\mathbf{X}^{2}&\ldots\mathbf{X}^{n}\end{pmatrix}\allowbreak\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ with $\mathbf{X}^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ being the rows generated independently:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}=\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{X}^{T}\left(\mathbf{I}_{n}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{n}\mathbf{1}_{n}^{T}}{n}\right)\mathbf{X} $$

Naturally, the quality of the denoiser (5) depends on the quality of approximation of the true covariance $\bm{\Sigma}$ by the empirical covariance (6). The latter does not have to be good in general, as $\bm{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ has $\Theta(d^{2})$ degrees of freedom and (6) attempts to estimate $\bm{\Sigma}$ from $n=\Theta(d)$ samples. As such, we would like to consider an alternative approach to minimizing (2) as well. The approach we propose is outlined below and is based on learning $\mathbf{W}$ directly from data, but the main technicality lies in how the training data should be generated from $\mathbf{X}$ .

We divide the training data $\mathbf{X}$ into $N$ batches $\mathbf{X}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times d},\dots,\mathbf{X}_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{N}\times d}$ In other words, $\mathbf{X}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times d},\dots,\mathbf{X}_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{N}\times d}$ are defined via $\mathbf{X}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{X}_{1}^{T}&\mathbf{X}_{2}^{T}&\ldots&\mathbf{X}_{N}^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ . Using $\mathbf{X}_{t}^{i}$ to denote the $i$ th row of $\mathbf{X}_{t}$ , note that the data points $\mathbf{X}^{i}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{X}^{i^{\prime}}_{t^{\prime}}$ are independent whenever $(i,t)\neq(i^{\prime},t^{\prime})$ and each row satisfies

$$ \mathbf{X}^{i}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\bm{\Sigma})\text{ for }t=1,\dots,N\text{ and }i=1,\dots,n_{t} $$

Furthermore, consider independent noise vectors

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{i}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\text{ where }\mathbf{Z}^{i}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\bm{\Sigma}_{t}),\text{ }t=1,\dots,N,i=1,\dots,n_{t} $$

We construct noisy data batches $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t}:=\mathbf{X}_{t}+\mathbf{Z}_{t},\text{ }t=1,\dots,N$ and train a denoiser $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}:=\argmin_{\mathbf{W}}\Bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\Bigr\|_{F}^{2} $$

Here, $\hat{\mathbf{X}}$ is the full noisy data matrix defined as $\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{1}^{T}&\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{2}^{T}&\ldots&\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{N}^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ . The main results of the present work, namely Theorems 1 and 5 in Section 3, address the following questions:

What is the generalization error (2) of the denoiser $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ found via (7) for given $N,n_{1},\dots,n_{t},d,\bm{\Sigma}_{1},\dots,\bm{\Sigma}_{N}$ ?

Focusing on the case of $N=1$ and relying on Theorem 1, we also conduct extensive mathematical (Corollary 3) as well as numerical (Section 5) investigations of the following questions:

What is the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ leading to the minimal generalization error (2) among linear denoisers trained via (7) in terms of $\bm{\Sigma}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ ? How can we approximate this optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ algorithmically given access only to $\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n}$ ? Can we outperform the empirical Wiener filter (5) using such an approximation of the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ ?

We will also impose the following technical assumptions that are necessary for our analyses.

#### Assumptions 1.

- 1. $\bm{\Sigma}$ is invertible.

- 2. $\frac{n_{t}}{d}\to\kappa_{t}>0$ as $n_{t},d\rightarrow\infty$ for each $t=1,\dots,N$ and $\kappa=\kappa_{1}+\dots+\kappa_{N}>1$ .

Our Main Contributions:

- • We characterize the generalization error of $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ found from (7) for arbitrary $N,n_{1},\dots,n_{t},d,\allowbreak\bm{\Sigma}_{1},\dots,\bm{\Sigma}_{N}$ satisfying Assumptions 1 in Theorem 5.

- • In the case of $N=1$ , we derive much more explicit results, which are formulated in Theorem 1, again assuming assumptions 1 hold.

- • We use Theorem 1 to find the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ minimizing the generalization error for the speciailized case when $N=1$ and both $\bm{\Sigma}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ are scalar. Perhaps surprisingly, even in this case we see that the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ is in general different from $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ , meaning it’s better to take different noise distributions for training and testing. The result is presented in Corollary 3.

- • In Section 5, we propose an algorithm for approximating the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ for the case $N=1$ and arbitrary $\bm{\Sigma},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ . This algorithm is based on Theorem 1. We then proceed to verify that in certain cases the $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ resulting from (7) indeed outperforms the empirical Wiener filter (5).

## 3 Main Results

Since we use CGMT, our results are asymptotic, meaning that we characterize the error $\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})$ via certain quantities $f_{n,d}$ , such that $\frac{\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})}{f_{n,d}}\to 1$ as $n,d\to\infty$ and $\frac{n}{d}\to\kappa>1$ . For the ease of exposition, we just write equalities within the results of this section, but keep the reference to the asymptotic regime in the formulation to avoid confusion. We would like to begin with stating the results we obtained for $N=1$ , as the expressions we get in this case are more explicit and thus allow for more insight.

#### Theorem 1.

Assume that $N=1$ and Assumptions 1 hold. Then, for the denoiser $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ found via (7), its generalization error (2) can be characterized asymptotically as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})=\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{n-d}\text{Tr}\Bigl[\Bigl(\bm{\Sigma}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(\bm{\Sigma}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\Bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr)\Bigl(\text{Tr}\Bigl[\bm{\Sigma}\Bigr]-\text{Tr}\Bigl[\Bigl(\bm{\Sigma}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}^{2}\Bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr) \displaystyle+\text{Tr}\Bigl[\Bigl(\bm{\Sigma}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}-\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)\Bigl(\bm{\Sigma}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}^{2}\Bigr] $$

*Figure 1: Phase Transition explained in Remark 4*

Specifying Theorem 1 to the case $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ leads to the following corollary:

#### Corollary 2.

Under the setting of Theorem 1, assume in addition that $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}$ commute. Then, for the denoiser found via (7), its generalization error (2) asymptotically equals the following, where $\cal{E}_{\text{Wiener}}$ denotes the generalization error (2) minimized over $\mathbf{W}$ , which is attained by the Wiener Filter (4):

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-1}\cal{E}_{\text{Wiener}} $$

Note that taking $\kappa\to\infty$ , i.e. assuming $n\gg d$ , recovers the performance of the Wiener filter. As expected, $\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})\geq\cal{E}_{\text{Wiener}}$ .

We obtain another corollary of Theorem 1 by treating the case of scalar $\bm{\Sigma}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ in greater detail:

#### Corollary 3.

Under the setting of Theorem 1, assume in addition that $\bm{\Sigma}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ are scalar matrices and define:

$$ \bm{\Sigma}=\frac{c}{d}\mathbf{I}_{d}\text{ and }\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}=\frac{c_{\mathbf{z}}}{d}\mathbf{I}_{d} $$

Then minimizing the generalization error (2) of the denoiser found via (7) over $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ leads to the following optimal generalization error:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\frac{-(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})^{2}+4(\kappa-1)^{2}cc_{\mathbf{z}}}{4(\kappa-2)(\kappa-1)(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}<0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}<0\\
\min\{c,c_{\mathbf{z}}\}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

#### Remark 4.

Corollary 3 reveals an interesting phase transition phenomenon, whose phase diagram is depicted in Fig. 1. In region I, defined by $3-2\kappa+\frac{c_{\mathbf{z}}}{c}>0$ , the generalization error equals $c_{\mathbf{z}}$ and the optimal $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}=\mathbf{I}_{d}$ regardless of the choice of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ . In region III, defined by $3-2\kappa+\frac{c}{c_{\mathbf{z}}}>0$ , the generalization error equals $c$ and the optimal $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}=0$ , again regardless of the choice of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ . The interesting region II, defined as the complement of I and III, is where there exists a unique $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ achieving the best performance and the resulting $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}\notin\{0,\mathbf{I}_{d}\}$ . We fixed $c=1$ for Fig. 1.

Finally, we formulate the expression that we have derived for the case of $N>1$ . The expression we obtain for $N>1$ is more complicated and we leave analyzing it further and making it more explicit as a subject for future work.

#### Theorem 5.

Suppose that Assumptions 1 hold. Consider $\{\theta_{t}\}_{t=1}^{N}$ found as the unique fixed points of the following system of equations

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{t} \displaystyle=2-2\theta_{t}\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}(\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\bm{\Sigma})\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\biggr] $$

Define

$$ \theta=2-4\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}(\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\bm{\Sigma})\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}\biggr] $$

Finally, consider the matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+2)\times(N+2)}$ defined in (25) and vector $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{N+2}$ defined in (27), deferred to the Appendix due to their longer descriptions. Then, for the denoiser $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ found via (7), its generalization error (2) can be characterized asymptotically as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})=\frac{1}{4(n-d)^{2}}(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b})_{N+2}+\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}(\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\bm{\Sigma})\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}(\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\bm{\Sigma})\Bigr)^{-1} \displaystyle\cdot\Bigl(4\theta^{2}(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b})_{1}\bm{\Sigma}+16(n-d)^{2}\bm{\Sigma}^{2}+\theta^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta^{2}_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b})_{t+1}\Bigr)\biggr] $$

Where $(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b})_{j}$ denotes the $j$ th entry of the vector $\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{N+2}$ .

## 4 Proof Technique and Sketches

Both proofs rely heavily on a result known in the literature as the Convex Gaussian Min-Max Theorem (CGMT). We refer the reader to Thrampoulidis et al. (2014); Akhtiamov et al. (2025a) for a formal detailed treatment of the CGMT, but we will outline it briefly for completeness. The goal of the CGMT is to analyze properties of solutions of the objectives of the following form, called the Primary Optimization (PO) objective:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}}}\max_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{u}}}\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{w}+\psi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w})\quad\textbf{(PO)} $$

Here, $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , $\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{u}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n},\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are compact convex sets, $\psi$ is convex in $\mathbf{u}$ and concave in $\mathbf{w}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ is an i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ matrix. To analyze (10), the CGMT framework introduces another objective, called Auxillary Objective (AO), where $\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ vectors:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}}}\max_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{u}}}\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{w}\|\mathbf{u}\|+\mathbf{h}^{T}\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{w}\|+\psi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w})\quad\textbf{(AO)} $$

Consider an arbitrary set $\mathbf{S}\subset\mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{w}}$ . Let $\mathbf{w}_{AO}$ and $\mathbf{w}_{PO}$ be any minimizers of (11) and (10) respectively. Assume that $\mathbf{w}_{AO}\in\mathbf{S}$ holds with probability approaching 1 (w.p.a. 1), i.e. :

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{w}_{AO}\in\mathbf{S}\right)\to 1\text{ as }n,d\to\infty $$

Then $\mathbf{w}_{PO}\in\mathbf{S}$ holds w.p.a. 1 as well, i.e.:

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{w}_{PO}\in\mathbf{S}\right)\to 1\text{ as }n,d\to\infty $$

Note that, formally speaking, we should introduce sequences of PO and AO to discuss convergence in probability. However, we suppress these formalities to ease exposition and refer the interested reader to Thrampoulidis et al. (2014); Akhtiamov et al. (2025a) for a rigorous exposition.

Sketch of the proof of Theorems 1 and 5: Recall that the linear denoiser $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ is defined via:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{W}}\Bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\Bigr\|_{F}^{2}=\min_{\mathbf{W}}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{I})+\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}\|_{F}^{2} $$

Denoting the $i$ -th column of $\mathbf{W}$ by $\mathbf{w}_{i}$ , we can rewrite (12) as:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min_{\mathbf{w}_{i}}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{w}_{i}-\mathbf{e}_{i})+\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}_{i}\|^{2} $$

Introducing a set of Fenchel dual variables $\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for $i=1,\dots,d$ and writing $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{G}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ , where $\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ is i.i.d. standard normal, we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min_{\mathbf{w}_{i}}\max_{\mathbf{v}_{i}}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{G}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}_{i}-\mathbf{e}_{i})+\mathbf{v}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}_{i}-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{4} $$

With a slight abuse of notation we drop the indices from $\mathbf{w}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{i}$ and rewrite:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min_{\mathbf{w}}\max_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{G}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i})+\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2}}{4} $$

Let $\mathbf{u}:=\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i})$ . Using a Lagrange multiplier and leveraging Sion’s minimax theorem:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\max_{\bm{\lambda}}\min_{\mathbf{w},\mathbf{u}}\max_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}+\bm{\lambda}^{T}\mathbf{u}-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i})-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2}}{4} $$

Treating each term of (14) as a separate PO with an i.i.d. standard normal $\mathbf{G}$ , we arrive at the following sum of AOs:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\max_{\bm{\lambda}}\min_{\mathbf{w},\mathbf{u}}\max_{\mathbf{v}}\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}\mathbf{h}^{T}\mathbf{v}+\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}+\bm{\lambda}^{T}\mathbf{u}-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i})-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2}}{4} $$

Denoting $\beta=\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}$ and performing optimization over the direction $\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\max_{\bm{\lambda}}\min_{\mathbf{w},\mathbf{u}}\max_{\beta>0}\beta\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{u}+\beta\Bigl\|\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}+\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}\mathbf{h}\Bigr\|_{2}+\bm{\lambda}^{T}\mathbf{u}-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i})-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4} $$

Denoting $\eta=\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}$ and optimizing over $\frac{\mathbf{u}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\max_{\bm{\lambda}}\min_{\mathbf{w},\eta>0}\max_{\beta>0}-\eta\|\beta\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}\|_{2}+\beta\Bigl\|\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}+\eta\mathbf{h}\Bigr\|_{2}-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i})-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4} $$

After swapping around min and max due to convexity-concavity by Lemma 6, we employ the square-root trick $\sqrt{x}=\min_{s>0}\frac{s}{2}+\frac{x}{2s}$ and obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\max_{\bm{\lambda}}\min_{\eta>0}\max_{\beta>0}-\eta\|\beta\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}\|_{2}-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4}+\min_{\mathbf{w},\tau>0}\frac{\beta\tau}{2}+\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl\|\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{w}+\eta\mathbf{h}\Bigr\|^{2}_{2}-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i}) $$

Now, recall the block structure we have for $\mathbf{Z}$ and introduce a matching structure for $\mathbf{h}$ , where each $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{t}}$ : $\mathbf{Z}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{Z}_{1}^{T}&\mathbf{Z}_{2}^{T}&\ldots&\mathbf{Z}_{N}^{T}\end{pmatrix}\text{ and }\mathbf{h}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{h}^{(1)T}&\mathbf{h}^{(2)T}&\ldots&\mathbf{h}^{(N)T}\end{pmatrix}$ . We arrive at:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\max_{\bm{\lambda}}\min_{\eta>0}\max_{\beta>0}-\eta\|\beta\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}\|_{2}-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4}+\min_{\mathbf{w},\tau>0}\frac{\beta\tau}{2}+\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\Bigl\|\mathbf{Z}_{t}\mathbf{w}+\eta\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\Bigr\|^{2}_{2}-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i}) $$

Using a Fenchel Dual $\mathbf{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{t}}$ for each $t=1,\dots,N$ , we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min_{\mathbf{w}}\max_{\mathbf{v}_{t}}\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\mathbf{v}_{t}^{T}\mathbf{Z}_{t}\mathbf{w}+\eta\mathbf{v}_{t}^{T}\mathbf{h}^{(t)}-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}{4}\Bigr)-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i}) $$

Applying CGMT again, but this time with respect to the randomness in $\mathbf{Z}^{(t)}$ , we can replace the inner optimization part of (15) by the following:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}}\max_{\mathbf{v}_{t}}\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\|\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}\|_{2}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{t}+\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|_{2}\mathbf{g}_{t}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}+\eta\mathbf{v}_{t}^{T}\mathbf{h}^{(t)}-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}{4}\Bigr)-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{i}) $$

We defer further analyses of (16) to the Appendix due to the lack of space, but we wanted to illustrate that the proofs of Theorems 1 and 5 proceed by a two-stage application of the CGMT followed by a meticuolous detailed analysis of (16).

## 5 Experiments

In this section we provide numerical experiments to corroborate our findings and discuss the proposed denoising algorithm.

### 5.1 Verifying Corollary 3 and Theorem 1

We begin with verifying Corollary 3. We take $\bm{\Sigma}=\mathbf{I}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}=\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=c_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}$ and plot the performance of the linear denoiser against $\kappa$ . We also use the closed-form expression obtained in (9) to plot the optimal generalization error from Corollary 3. Furthermore, we investigate how the error changes if we replace the Gaussian features with Rademacher with the same the first and second moments. The results are reported in Fig. 2, where cross marks denote the simulated values and solid-lines depict the predictions coming from Corollary 3. We observe a close match between our predictions and the simulated errors for the Gaussian features as well as a close match between the generalization errors for Gaussian and Rademacher features. The latter suggests a form of universality, which we propose as a direction for future work.

To verify Theorem 1 for a non-scalar $\bm{\Sigma}$ , we generated $n$ synthetic data points of dimension $d=50$ distributed i.i.d. according to $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\bm{\Sigma})$ where $\bm{\Sigma}_{ij}=\delta_{ij}i^{-4},i,j=1,\dots,d$ (the power law exponent $4$ is chosen arbitrarily without any specific consideration in mind). For simplicity, we set $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}=\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=\mathbf{I}$ . We vary the number of samples $n$ by changing $\kappa$ and train the denoiser via solving the least-squares objective through the linear system of equations by Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions. For each $\kappa$ , we evaluate the generalization error of the trained denoiser and compare it with our predictions from Theorem 1. Finally, we also approximated the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ dictated by the expression (8) from Theorem 1 via the following heuristics: we initialize $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ and then performed projected gradient descent on $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ . To make sure $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ stays PSD, we fixed the basis of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ to be the basis of $\bm{\Sigma}$ and trained vector of the eigenvalues of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ via gradient descent with projection on the positive orthant. The results are reported in Fig. 3 where cross marks denote the simulated values and solid-lines depict the predictions coming from Theorem 1. We observe a close match between the theory and the simulated values as well as that optimizing over $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ does increase performance.

### 5.2 Heuristics for using the result of Theorem 1 for training denoisers

Since, in practice, $\bm{\Sigma}$ is not known, we propose to use the sample covariance (6) and perform the following optimization as a surrogate of the expression (8) from Theorem 1:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\succeq\mathbf{0}}\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{n-d}\text{Tr}\Bigl(\Bigl(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\Bigr)\Bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl(\text{Tr}\Bigl(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}\Bigr)-\text{Tr}\Bigl(\Bigl(\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{2}\Bigr)\Bigr)\Bigr) $$

Since the problem (17) is not convex in $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ , solving it precisely appears out of reach, so we suggest the following heuristics. We initialize $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}$ and, to make sure $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ stays PSD, we fix the basis of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ to be the basis of $\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}$ and train the vector of the eigenvalues of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ via gradient descent with projection on the positive orthant. The performance of the true Wiener filter is depicted using dashed-lines and serves as a baseline for performance. To demonstrate that it is possible to outperform the empirical Wiener filter, we consider the case where $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{I}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}=c^{2}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{T}$ , with $c>0$ being the scaling factor and $\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ having i.i.d. standard normal entries. We choose a non-diagonal $\bm{\Sigma}$ to ensure that it cannot be estimated reliably from $\Theta(d)$ samples. We vary $c$ and plot the performance of the empirical filter against the performance of $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ with optimized $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ in Figure 4. We also have included the performance of the Wiener filter and the $\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}$ denoiser. As we increase $c$ , we observe that performance of the empirical and true Wiener filters and our proposed filter approaches that of the identity denoiser. We see that, for large values of $c$ , i.e. the high SNR regime, $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ outperforms the empirical Wiener filter.

## 6 Conclusion and Future Directions

In this work we rigorously derived the precise asymptotics of a linear denoiser trained using the least-squares objective in the proportional regime. Possible future directions include investigating the expressions obtained in Theorem 5 to understand how using different batches of data may help with the performance. Another promising direction is to extend the analysis to the overparameterized regime where the number of parameters exceed the number of samples and the denoiser is trained via SGD or via a regularized objective.

While we maintained the assumption of data gaussianity throughout the present work, we suspect it is not necessary for Theorems 1 and 5. As has been observed in the literature for many statistical inference problems, the generalization error often depends only on the first and second order statistics of the data, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Gaussian Universality (see (Pesce et al., 2023; Ghane et al., 2024) and references therein). In addition, Figure 2 suggests that a form of universality might hold for the denoisers trained through the least-squares objective too. We leave the latter as an interesting direction for future work.

## Appendix A Proof of Theorems 1 and 5: common part

Here we describe the proof in full detail. We start with the objective (16) obtained in the main body and take $i=1$ WLOG:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}}\max_{\mathbf{v}_{t}}\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\|\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}\|_{2}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{t}+\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|_{2}\mathbf{g}_{t}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}+\eta\mathbf{v}_{t}^{T}\mathbf{h}^{(t)}-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}{4}\Bigr)-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{1}) $$

Doing the optimization over the direction of $\mathbf{v}_{t}$ yields:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}}\max_{\beta_{t}>0}\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\beta_{t}\Bigl\|\eta\mathbf{h}^{(t)}+\|\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}\|_{2}\mathbf{h}_{t}\Bigr\|_{2}+\beta_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}-\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}}{4}\Bigr)-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{1}) $$

Using the square-root trick, we introduce the variables $\tau_{t}$ for $1\leq t\leq N$ :

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}}\max_{\beta_{t}>0}\min_{\tau_{t}>0} \displaystyle\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}\tau_{t}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{t}}{2\tau_{t}}\Bigl(\eta^{2}n_{t}+\|\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}\|^{2}_{2}n_{t}\Bigr)+\beta_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{w}-\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}}{4}\Bigr) \displaystyle-\bm{\lambda}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{e}_{1}) $$

Performing the optimization over $\bm{\lambda}$ yields the following scalar optimization:

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\tau_{\lambda}>0}\min_{\eta>0}\max_{\beta>0} \displaystyle-\frac{\eta\tau_{\lambda}}{2}-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4}+\min_{\tau>0}\frac{\beta\tau}{2}+\max_{\beta_{t}}\min_{\tau_{t}}\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}\tau_{t}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{t}}{2\tau_{t}}\eta^{2}n_{t}-\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}}{4}\Bigr) \displaystyle-\beta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{T}\Bigl(\frac{2\tau_{\lambda}}{\eta}\mathbf{I}+\frac{\beta}{\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}}{\tau_{t}}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\Bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{g} \displaystyle-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4\tau^{2}}\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\beta_{t}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{g}_{t}\Bigr)^{T}\Bigl(\frac{2\tau_{\lambda}}{\eta}\mathbf{I}+\frac{\beta}{\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}}{\tau_{t}}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\Bigr)^{-1} \displaystyle\cdot\sum_{t=1}^{N}\beta_{t}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{g}_{t} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac{\eta}{2\tau_{\lambda}}\mathbf{I}+\frac{1}{4}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac{\beta}{2\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}}{2\tau_{t}}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{e}_{1} $$

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{2}F\Bigl(\frac{\beta}{\tau},\frac{\beta_{t}}{\tau_{t}},\frac{\eta}{\tau_{\lambda}},\beta,\beta_{t}\Bigr) \displaystyle=-\frac{\beta n_{t}}{\tau}\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(\frac{2\tau_{\lambda}}{\eta}\bm{\Sigma}+\frac{\beta}{\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}}{\tau_{t}}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{t} \displaystyle\cdot\Bigl(\frac{2\tau_{\lambda}}{\eta}\bm{\Sigma}+\frac{\beta}{\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_{t}}{\tau_{t}}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(\beta^{2}\bm{\Sigma}+\frac{\beta^{2}}{4\tau^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\beta^{2}_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\frac{\tau_{\lambda}^{2}}{\eta^{2}}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{e}_{1}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}\Bigr)\biggr] $$

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\theta}{2} \displaystyle=1-2\theta\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(\frac{2}{\zeta}\bm{\Sigma}+\theta\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}\biggr] #### Lemma 6.

The function $f(\beta):=\|\beta\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}\|_{2}$ for $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and any $\mathbf{g},\bm{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is convex in $\beta\in[0,\infty)$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by verifying the definition of convexity. Let $0\leq t\leq 1$ , then for any $\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\geq 0$ we have

$$ \displaystyle tf(\beta_{1})+(1-t)f(\beta_{2}) \displaystyle=\|t\beta_{1}\mathbf{g}+t\bm{\lambda}\|_{2}+\|(1-t)\beta_{1}\mathbf{g}+(1-t)\bm{\lambda}\|_{2} \displaystyle\geq\|((t\beta_{1}+(1-t)\beta_{2})\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}\|_{2} $$

Where the inequality follows by the convexity of $\ell_{2}$ on vectors $\beta_{1}\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}$ and $\beta_{2}\mathbf{g}+\bm{\lambda}$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle tf(\beta_{1})+(1-t)f(\beta_{2})\geq f(t\beta_{1}+(1-t)\beta_{2}) $$

And the result follows. ∎

### A.3 Proof of Concentration of the Generalization Error

In this section, we would like to show that one can use the concentration of some scalar functions of $\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\ast}$ for $j=1,\ldots,d$ to prove the concentration of the total generalization error of $\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}}$ . Namely, by the prior arguments, we have observed that $\|\bm{\Sigma}_{j}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}_{j}-\mathbf{e}_{j})\|^{2}_{2}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\zeta^{2}\tau_{\lambda}^{(j)2}$ for each $j=1,\ldots,d$ . Moreover, one can specifiy the concentration rate, similar to Dokmanic and Gribonval (2019); Hassani and Javanmard (2024), where one can show that there exist $c_{1},c_{2}=\theta(1)$ such that for $t_{j}>0$ for $i\in[d]$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\Bigl|d\|\bm{\Sigma}_{j}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}_{j}-\mathbf{e}_{j})\|^{2}_{2}-d\zeta^{2}\tau_{\lambda}^{(j)2}\Bigr|>t_{j}\Bigr)\leq c_{1}\exp(-c_{2}dt_{j}) $$

Furthermore, let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{j}:=\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(\theta\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\frac{2}{\zeta}\bm{\Sigma}\Bigr)^{-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}} \displaystyle\Bigl(\theta\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta_{t}n_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}+\frac{2}{\zeta}\bm{\Sigma}\Bigr)^{-1} \displaystyle\cdot\Bigl(4\theta^{2}\tau^{2}\bm{\Sigma}+\frac{4}{\zeta^{2}}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{e}_{j}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}+\theta^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\theta^{2}_{t}\tau^{(j)2}_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\Bigr)\biggr] $$

We have similarly for $c_{3},c_{4}=\theta(1)$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\Bigl|d\mathbf{w}^{\ast T}_{j}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{w}^{\ast}_{j}-d\mathcal{L}_{j}\Bigr|>t_{j}\Bigr)\leq c_{3}\exp(-c_{4}dt_{j}) $$

Note that we had

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\mathbf{w}^{\ast T}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\ast}+(\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\ast}-\mathbf{e}_{j})^{T}\bm{\Sigma}_{j}(\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\ast}-\mathbf{e}_{j}) $$

The concentration of the solutions follows by a union bound argument, from:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\Bigl|\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{lsq}})-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\mathcal{L}_{j}+\zeta^{2}\tau_{\lambda}^{(j)2}\Bigr|>t\Bigr)\leq\sum_{j=1}^{d}\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\Bigl|\mathbf{w}^{\ast T}_{j}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{w}^{\ast}_{j}-\mathcal{L}_{j}+\|\bm{\Sigma}_{j}^{1/2}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}_{j}-\mathbf{e}_{j})\|^{2}_{2}-\zeta^{2}\tau_{\lambda}^{(j)2}\Bigr|>\frac{t}{d}\Bigr) \displaystyle\leq 2d\max\{c_{1},c_{3}\}\exp(-\min\{c_{2},c_{4}\}dt) $$

Thus the statement follows as $t=\omega(1)$ .

## Appendix B Proof of Corollary 3

We consider $\bm{\Sigma}=c\mathbf{I}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}=c_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}$ and write

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\succeq\mathbf{0}} \displaystyle\Bigl(1+\frac{c+c_{\mathbf{z}}}{n-d}\text{Tr}\Bigl(c\mathbf{I}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigr)\Bigl(cd-c^{2}\text{Tr}\Bigl(c\mathbf{I}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigr) \displaystyle+c^{2}\text{Tr}\biggl[\Bigl(c\mathbf{I}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(c_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}-\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)\Bigl(c\mathbf{I}+\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\Bigr)^{-1}\biggr] $$

Note that, since the KKT condition for the optimal $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ is symmetric w.r.t. the eigenvalues of $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}$ in this case, we can take $\bm{\Sigma}_{1}=\sigma\mathbf{I}$ , which leads to

$$ \displaystyle c\cdot \displaystyle\min_{\sigma\geq 0}\Bigl(1+\frac{d}{n-d}\frac{c+c_{\mathbf{z}}}{c+\sigma}\Bigr)\Bigl(d-d\frac{c}{c+\sigma}\Bigr)+cd\frac{c_{\mathbf{z}}-\sigma}{(c+\sigma)^{2}} \displaystyle=cd\cdot\min_{\sigma\geq 0}1+\frac{\frac{d(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}{n-d}-c}{c+\sigma}+\frac{-c\frac{d(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}{n-d}+c(c_{\mathbf{z}}-\sigma)}{(c+\sigma)^{2}} \displaystyle=cd+cd\cdot\min_{\sigma\geq 0}\frac{-c\frac{d(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}{n-d}+c(c_{\mathbf{z}}-\sigma)+\Bigl(\frac{d(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}{n-d}-c\Bigr)(c+\sigma)}{(c+\sigma)^{2}} \displaystyle=cd+cd\cdot\min_{\sigma\geq 0}\frac{\Bigl(\frac{d(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}{n-d}-2c\Bigr)\sigma+cc_{\mathbf{z}}-c^{2}}{(c+\sigma)^{2}} $$

Then we observe for the optimal $\sigma$

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{\ast}=\begin{cases}0&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}<0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}>0\\
c\frac{c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}}{(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}}&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}<0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}<0\\
\infty&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}<0\\
\infty&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c_{\mathbf{z}}>c\\
0&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c_{\mathbf{z}}<c\end{cases} $$

In each case, the best generalization error turns out to be

$$ \displaystyle g.e\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\begin{cases}dc_{\mathbf{z}}&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}<0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}>0\\
d\frac{-(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})^{2}+4(\kappa-1)^{2}cc_{\mathbf{z}}}{4(\kappa-2)(\kappa-1)(c+c_{\mathbf{z}})}&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}<0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}<0\\
dc&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}<0\\
dc&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c_{\mathbf{z}}>c\\
dc_{\mathbf{z}}&(3-2\kappa)c+c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c+(3-2\kappa)c_{\mathbf{z}}>0,\quad c_{\mathbf{z}}<c\end{cases} $$
